title: Sloppy Joe
subtitle: Sweet-spiced beef mince in tomato sauce on a soft bun
excerpt: A Sloppy Joe is seasoned beef mince simmered in a sweet, tomatoey sauce until it is thick enough to pile onto a soft bun without running off entirely. The sauce has ketchup, Worcestershire, a little brown sugar, and vinegar. It is deliberately messy and deliberately good.
sourceNotes: American midcentury comfort food. The Sloppy Joe is claimed by several Midwestern diners, the most common story placing its origin at a café in Sioux City, Iowa, in the 1930s. Fannie Farmer, The Boston Cooking-School Cook Book (1896), Project Gutenberg, gives the baseline minced-beef-with-sauce method.

recipe.freezeNotes: The meat sauce freezes well in portions for up to 3 months. Thaw overnight in the fridge and reheat gently in a pan with a splash of water.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the recipe easily. The sauce keeps in the fridge for 3 days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The sauce is better the next day once the flavours have settled.

content.text: A Sloppy Joe is beef mince cooked down in a tangy tomato sauce of ketchup, Worcestershire, brown sugar, and vinegar until the sauce is thick and clingy. The result goes into a soft white bun. The name describes what happens when you eat it, and that is part of the appeal.

Heat {{vegetable-oil}} of vegetable oil in the pan over medium-high heat. Add {{beef-mince}} of beef mince and cook, breaking it up with a spoon, for 6 to 8 minutes until well browned and the liquid has evaporated. Tip out any excess fat.
Add the {{onion}} onion and {{pepper-green}} green pepper. Cook for 4 minutes until softened. Add {{garlic}} of garlic and the {{tomato-puree}} of tomato purée. Cook for 1 minute.

Add the {{ketchup}} of ketchup, {{worcestershire-sauce}} of Worcestershire sauce, {{light-brown-sugar}} of brown sugar, {{cider-vinegar}} of cider vinegar, {{mustard-powder}} of mustard powder, and 100 ml of water. Stir well. Simmer over medium-low heat for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce is thick and coats the mince. Season with salt.
Split and toast the buns lightly if you like. Pile the meat sauce into the buns and serve.

items.cause: Not simmered long enough, or mince was wet and released excess liquid.
items.fix: Simmer uncovered on medium-low for a further 5 minutes, stirring regularly, until the sauce tightens.

items.cause: Sugar ratio too high relative to the vinegar.
items.fix: Add a teaspoon more cider vinegar and a small pinch of chilli flakes to balance.

items.cause: Not broken up finely enough during browning.
items.fix: Use the back of a wooden spoon or a potato masher to break up any clumps while the mince cooks.
Reduce the sauce further before filling. The sauce should hold its shape on a spoon.

content.text: Turkey or chicken mince both work. Add a teaspoon of smoked paprika or dried chipotle chilli for a smoky note. Serve over jacket potatoes instead of buns for a lower-carb take. A handful of grated cheddar on top of the filling before the bun lid goes on is not traditional but it is very good.

The Sloppy Joe belongs to the American school cafeteria, the Tuesday-night family dinner, and the casual diner that doesn't pretend to be anything it isn't. The name is the recipe: it is intended to be messy. It became a staple partly because it stretches a small amount of mince across four portions and takes under half an hour.
